title: India | PMLA and RBI KYC Directions: AML/CFT Compliance
tagline: Apply India's AML/CFT rules at a commercial bank: PMLA 2002, the PML Rules, RBI's KYC Directions 2025, FIU-IND reporting and sanctions.
sectors: Retail, branch and digital onboarding teams
Payments, remittance and correspondent banking teams
Bank compliance, risk and internal audit functions
description:
This quest teaches staff of Indian commercial banks the country's own AML/CFT regime: the **Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)**, the **PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**, and the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025**, which RBI issued on 28 November 2025 and keeps updated. It also covers reporting to the **Financial Intelligence Unit – India (FIU-IND)** and the sanctions procedures under UAPA section 51A and WMD Act section 12A.

Paragraph 79 of the KYC Directions requires an ongoing training programme on the bank's KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline, compliance and onboarding staff. This quest is built for that audience, and for managers, auditors and directors with oversight roles.

Across five stages you follow a fictional team at Kaveri Meridian Bank in Mumbai, Pune, Kochi and New Delhi through customer acceptance and CDD, beneficial ownership, CKYCR, V-CIP, risk categorisation, PEPs, periodic updation, CTRs and STRs, tipping off, records, sanctions screening, wire transfers, correspondent banking, the Designated Director and Principal Officer, and real RBI and FIU-IND penalties.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own KYC/AML policies, procedures or advice from your compliance team.
audience: Branch, front-desk and contact centre staff at Indian commercial banks
Account opening, digital onboarding and V-CIP officials who perform customer due diligence
Payments, remittance, treasury and correspondent banking staff
Transaction monitoring analysts and the Principal Officer's team who prepare reports to FIU-IND
Managers, internal auditors, the Designated Director and Board members with AML/CFT oversight
outcomes: Explain how the PMLA 2002, the PML Rules 2005 and RBI's KYC Directions 2025 fit together, and the roles of RBI, FIU-IND, the Designated Director and the Principal Officer
Apply the Customer Acceptance Policy, identification triggers, beneficial ownership tests and CKYCR rules
Run risk categorisation, V-CIP, enhanced due diligence for non-face-to-face customers and PEPs, and periodic updation of KYC
File the right reports with FIU-IND on time, avoid tipping off and keep records for the required periods
Apply sanctions screening, wire transfer and correspondent banking rules, and describe the programme RBI and FIU-IND expect

quest.name: The Rupee Trail
quest.premise: You have joined the AML/CFT compliance team at Kaveri Meridian Bank, a fictional Indian commercial bank, just as RBI's new KYC Directions bed in. With Principal Officer Meera Iyer, analyst Arjun Malhotra, branch manager Farhan Qureshi, V-CIP lead Kavya Reddy and Designated Director Vikram Desai, you must follow the trail of suspicious money from the counter to FIU-IND and get the bank ready for its audit.

badge.name: Rupee Trail Guardian
badge.description: Awarded for demonstrating working knowledge of India's PMLA, PML Rules and RBI KYC Directions as they apply to commercial banks.

sessions.title: PMLA 2002, the PML Rules and the RBI KYC Directions
sessions.summary: Map India's AML/CFT rulebook: the Prevention of Money-laundering Act 2002, the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules 2005, RBI's KYC Directions 2025, FIU-IND, the Designated Director and Principal Officer, staff training and the penalties that follow failures.
objectives: Explain how the PMLA 2002, the PML Rules 2005 and the RBI KYC Directions 2025 fit together for a commercial bank
Describe the roles of RBI, FIU-IND, the Board, the Designated Director and the Principal Officer
Outline the money-laundering offence and the penalty powers of the Director, FIU-IND and of RBI
State what paragraph 79 of the KYC Directions requires for staff screening and training

cards.title: Stage one: the rulebook vault
cards.setting: Compliance floor, Kaveri Meridian Bank head office, Bandra Kurla Complex, Mumbai. 9:10 am.

lines.text: Your first morning at Kaveri Meridian Bank. Your badge says 'AML/CFT Compliance' and your inbox already holds an FIU-IND circular and an RBI inspection follow-up.
Welcome! I'm Meera Iyer, the bank's Principal Officer. Every report we send to FIU-IND goes out under my name.
Arjun Malhotra, transaction monitoring. I live in the alert queue. Some days it feels like the alerts live in me.
(on video from Pune) Farhan Qureshi, branch manager, Shivajinagar. My tellers ask me one question daily: which rule says we have to do all this?
Vikram Desai, whole-time director. The Board named me Designated Director, so I answer for the bank's PMLA compliance. I want to know we are on solid ground.
So your first mission is the map: the Act, the Rules, RBI's Directions, who does what, and what happens when a bank gets it wrong.
Five stages, one final exam. By the end you should be able to explain our duties to a teller, an analyst and a director. Ready?

scenes.heading: The Act
scenes.narration: The Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 creates the money-laundering offence and, in its Chapter Four, places record-keeping and reporting duties on reporting entities. Every bank is a reporting entity.

scenes.heading: The Rules
scenes.narration: The Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 fill in the detail: which transactions must be recorded and reported, when reports are due, and how client due diligence works.

scenes.heading: RBI's Directions
scenes.narration: On 28 November 2025 RBI replaced its old KYC Master Direction with entity-wise Directions. Commercial banks now follow the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, kept updated as amendments arrive.

scenes.heading: FIU-IND
scenes.narration: The Financial Intelligence Unit – India receives cash, suspicious and other prescribed reports, analyses them and passes intelligence to enforcement agencies. Its Director can also penalise reporting entities that fail their duties.

scenes.heading: Your bank's policy
scenes.narration: Each bank turns all of this into a Board-approved KYC policy. That policy, and the procedures under it, are what you apply at the counter and in the back office.

cards.title: From Parliament to your desk
cards.caption: Each layer must stay consistent with the one above it. The Directions apply to commercial banks, other than small finance, payments and local area banks.

items.label: PMLA 2002
items.detail: Offence of money laundering; Chapter IV duties of reporting entities; FIU-IND powers.

items.label: PML Rules 2005
items.detail: Records, reports, deadlines and client due diligence in detail.

items.label: RBI KYC Directions 2025
items.detail: How commercial banks must apply KYC, CDD, monitoring, reporting and sanctions duties.

items.label: Board-approved KYC policy
items.detail: Customer acceptance, risk management, identification and transaction monitoring.

items.label: Procedures and training
items.detail: What each team does every day, taught through an ongoing training programme.

cards.question: A colleague says the RBI KYC Directions 2025 are 'just guidance' because the real law is the PMLA. What is the best answer?
options: The Directions are binding RBI instructions that tell banks how to meet their PMLA and PML Rules duties
The Directions are optional best practice that banks may adopt if they choose
The Directions replaced the PMLA for banks when they were issued in 2025
The Directions only apply to banks' overseas branches and subsidiaries
cards.explanation: RBI issues the Directions to commercial banks, and RBI can penalise non-compliance. They implement the Act and Rules rather than replace them; overseas branches follow them too, applying the stricter standard where host rules differ.

cards.title: Designated Director and Principal Officer
cards.caption: Paragraphs 14 and 15 of the KYC Directions; the PML Rules name the Principal Officer as the officer who furnishes information to the Director, FIU-IND.

items.label: Who
items.left: A Managing Director or whole-time director the Board authorises
items.right: A nominated officer at management level

items.label: Answers for
items.left: Overall compliance with Chapter IV of the PMLA and the Rules
items.right: Compliance, transaction monitoring, and sharing and reporting information

items.label: Reports to FIU-IND
items.left: Is accountable, but does not file reports
items.right: Files the prescribed reports under Rule 8

items.label: Name given to
items.left: FIU-IND and RBI
items.right: FIU-IND and RBI

items.label: Same person?
items.left: Cannot be the Principal Officer
items.right: Cannot be named Designated Director

cards.title: The offence and the penalties
cards.body:
**The offence.** Under the PMLA, money laundering covers any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime, such as concealing, possessing, acquiring or using them, or projecting or claiming them as untainted. It is treated as continuing for as long as someone keeps enjoying those proceeds.

**Punishment.** Section 4 provides rigorous imprisonment of at least three and up to seven years plus a fine, with a higher ceiling of ten years for certain scheduled offences.

**Failures by the bank.** Under section 13, the Director, FIU-IND can inquire into a reporting entity and then:
- issue a written warning;
- direct it to follow specific instructions or send progress reports;
- impose a penalty of **₹10,000 to ₹1 lakh for each failure** on the bank, its designated director or any employee.

Appeals go to the Appellate Tribunal. **RBI** separately penalises banks for breaching its Directions under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

cards.title: Who does what?
cards.prompt: Match each player in India's regime to its role.

pairs.right: Issues the KYC Directions to commercial banks, inspects them and imposes penalties for breaches
Receives and analyses CTRs, STRs and other reports and can penalise reporting entities under section 13
Approves the KYC policy and receives the outcome of the ML/TF risk assessment
Ensures the bank's overall compliance with the PMLA's reporting-entity duties
Monitors transactions and furnishes the bank's reports to the Director, FIU-IND
Receives quarterly audit notes on KYC/AML compliance

lines.text: A consultant suggested a saving: make Meera both Principal Officer and Designated Director. One role, one salary line.
It sounds efficient, but the Directions say the bank must not nominate the Principal Officer as Designated Director.
And the consultant also wants to outsource our KYC sign-off to a vendor in Bengaluru.
Outsourcing the work is possible within RBI's outsourcing rules. Outsourcing the decision on whether KYC is compliant is not.
Then help me write a clear answer for the Board.

cards.title: Advising the Board
cards.situation: The Board's risk committee asks you for a one-line recommendation on the consultant's two ideas: (1) combine the Principal Officer and Designated Director roles; (2) let a vendor decide whether customer KYC meets the bank's norms.

choices.text: Reject both: the roles must be held by different people, and the bank may not outsource decisions on KYC compliance.
choices.outcome: Correct. The Directions bar the Principal Officer from being Designated Director and say banks must not outsource the decision-making on KYC compliance. The vendor can support processing under the bank's control.

choices.text: Accept the combined role but keep KYC decisions in-house.
choices.outcome: Half right. Keeping KYC decisions in-house is correct, but combining the two roles breaks an express rule in the Directions.

choices.text: Accept both, provided the Board approves them in writing.
choices.outcome: Board approval cannot override the Directions. Both ideas conflict with RBI's express requirements.

choices.text: Accept both, but tell FIU-IND and RBI the new names.
choices.outcome: Notifying names is required for each role, but it does not cure a prohibited arrangement.

cards.front: Myth: only the compliance team has PMLA duties.
cards.back: Fact: the Rules make it the duty of the bank, its designated director, officers and employees to follow the procedures for maintaining and furnishing information.

cards.front: Myth: FIU-IND only collects reports; it cannot fine banks.
cards.back: Fact: section 13 lets the Director, FIU-IND warn, direct and fine a reporting entity, its designated director or employees.

cards.front: Myth: the KYC policy can be signed off by the Principal Officer.
cards.back: Fact: the Board, or a committee it delegates, must approve the KYC policy.

cards.front: Myth: overseas branches follow only host-country rules.
cards.back: Fact: the Directions apply to overseas branches and majority-owned subsidiaries; where standards differ, the stricter one applies.

cards.front: Myth: training once at induction is enough.
cards.back: Fact: paragraph 79 requires an ongoing training programme, with a different focus for frontline, compliance and onboarding staff.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four key elements RBI requires in a bank's KYC policy?
options: Customer Acceptance Policy
Risk management
Monitoring of transactions
Product pricing policy
cards.explanation: The four elements are the Customer Acceptance Policy, risk management, Customer Identification Procedures and monitoring of transactions. Pricing is outside the KYC policy.

cards.title: Real case: FIU-IND orders training at a co-operative bank (2024)
cards.body:
After an RBI inspection, RBI shared findings with FIU-IND that **The Utkal Co-operative Bank Ltd.** had not filed cash transaction reports and suspicious transaction reports on various accounts.

FIU-IND issued a show-cause notice, heard the bank and, by Order-in-Original No. 06/DIR/FIU-IND/2024 dated 9 February 2024, imposed a penalty of **₹1 lakh** under section 13(2)(d) for breaching section 12 of the PMLA and Rules 3 and 7.

The Director also **directed the bank to give suitable AML/CFT training to the staff concerned**.

**Lessons for you:**
- RBI and FIU-IND work together: inspection findings travel.
- Failing to file a CTR is a breach in itself, even without any suspicion.
- Regulators see training gaps as a root cause and can order a fix.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: The PMLA 2002 sets the offence and reporting-entity duties; the PML Rules 2005 set records, reports and deadlines; RBI's KYC Directions 2025 tell commercial banks how to comply.
The Board approves the KYC policy, which has four elements: customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification and transaction monitoring.
The Designated Director answers for overall PMLA compliance; the Principal Officer monitors and reports to FIU-IND. They must be different people.
FIU-IND can fine ₹10,000 to ₹1 lakh per failure; RBI penalises breaches of its Directions under the Banking Regulation Act.
Paragraph 79 requires Know Your Employee screening and ongoing KYC/AML/CFT training tailored to frontline, compliance and onboarding staff.

cards.prompt: Think of your own role. Which of the people in this stage (Principal Officer, Designated Director, Board, auditors) would you go to first with a KYC question, and do you know their name at your institution?

quiz.question: Which instrument contains the offence of money laundering and the punishment for it in India?
options: The PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
The RBI KYC Directions, 2025
The Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
quiz.explanation: The PMLA defines the offence (section 3) and sets the punishment (section 4). The Rules and the Directions deal with records, reporting and KYC procedures.

quiz.question: Kaveri Meridian Bank wants to name its Principal Officer as Designated Director too. What do the KYC Directions say?
options: The bank must not nominate the Principal Officer as Designated Director
It is allowed if the Board approves the dual role
It is allowed only for banks with fewer than 100 branches
It is required, so that one person owns PMLA compliance
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 14 of the Directions expressly bars the bank from nominating the Principal Officer as Designated Director. Board approval or bank size does not change this.

quiz.question: Who must approve a commercial bank's KYC policy?
options: The Principal Officer, after consulting FIU-IND
The Board of Directors, or a committee to which it has delegated the power
RBI's regional office, before the policy takes effect
The head of retail banking, with the CFO's sign-off
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 6 requires a KYC policy approved by the Board or a Board-delegated committee. RBI does not pre-approve it and the Principal Officer cannot approve it.

quiz.question: During an inquiry, the Director, FIU-IND finds that a bank employee repeatedly ignored the reporting procedure. Which action is available under section 13 of the PMLA?
options: Rigorous imprisonment of the employee for three to seven years
Cancellation of the bank's licence by FIU-IND
A penalty fixed at 1% of the bank's annual profit
A penalty of ₹10,000 to ₹1 lakh for each failure, which may be imposed on the employee
quiz.explanation: Section 13 lets the Director warn, direct, require reports and impose ₹10,000 to ₹1 lakh per failure on the entity, its designated director or employees. Imprisonment is for the offence under section 4, and licensing belongs to RBI.

quiz.question: What does paragraph 79 of the KYC Directions require about staff training?
options: A one-time course at induction, refreshed only if RBI issues new rules
Annual external certification of every employee by FIU-IND
An ongoing programme on the KYC/AML/CFT policy, with a different focus for frontline, compliance and onboarding staff
Training for compliance staff only, since others follow procedures
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 79 requires ongoing training adapted to frontline staff, compliance staff and staff dealing with new customers, plus special training for front-desk staff on customer-education issues.

quiz.question: Kaveri Meridian's branch in Dubai finds that the local AML rule on a point is stricter than RBI's. Which standard should the branch apply?
options: RBI's standard, because the bank is Indian
The host-country standard, because local law always prevails
Whichever standard the branch head considers more practical
The stricter of the two standards
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 4 applies the Directions to overseas branches and majority-owned subsidiaries and requires the more stringent standard where RBI and host-country rules differ.

quiz.question: To whom must the bank communicate the name, designation and contact details of its Designated Director and Principal Officer?
options: RBI only
The Ministry of Home Affairs and FIU-IND
SEBI and the Indian Banks' Association
FIU-IND and RBI
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 14 and 15 require the bank to give the details of both officers to FIU-IND and RBI.

quiz.question: An auditor notes that Kaveri Meridian has engaged a vendor that both processes KYC files and makes the final call on whether each customer's KYC is compliant. What is the problem?
options: Vendors may not see customer documents under any circumstances
Outsourcing any KYC work needs prior approval from FIU-IND
Banks must not outsource the decision-making on KYC compliance
There is no problem if the vendor is located in India
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 13 says the bank must not outsource the decision-making functions of determining compliance with KYC norms. Supporting work can be outsourced within RBI's outsourcing rules.

quiz.question: Which body receives the bank's quarterly audit notes and compliance on KYC/AML?
options: The Audit Committee
The Principal Officer's team
The FIU-IND Director
The bank's statutory central auditors
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 12 lists independent evaluation, concurrent or internal audit, and submission of quarterly audit notes and compliance to the Audit Committee.

quiz.question: In 2024 FIU-IND penalised The Utkal Co-operative Bank Ltd. for failing to file CTRs and STRs. What else did the Director order?
options: Closure of all accounts that had been missed
Replacement of the bank's Board of Directors
A ban on opening new accounts for one year
Suitable AML/CFT training for the staff concerned
quiz.explanation: FIU-IND's order summary records a ₹1 lakh penalty and a direction to provide suitable AML/CFT training to the concerned staff.

sessions.title: Customer acceptance, identification and due diligence
sessions.summary: Apply RBI's Customer Acceptance Policy, the triggers for customer identification, the officially valid documents, the beneficial ownership tests of the PML Rules, reliance on third parties and the Central KYC Records Registry.
objectives: Apply the Customer Acceptance Policy rules, including when not to open an account and when to consider an STR
Recognise when customer identification is required, including the ₹50,000 walk-in threshold and structuring
Identify beneficial owners of companies, partnerships, associations and trusts using the PML Rules thresholds
Use the Central KYC Records Registry correctly, including the KYC Identifier and upload timelines

cards.title: Stage two: the onboarding gate
cards.setting: Shivajinagar branch, Pune. 11:20 am, a busy Monday.

lines.text: Three cases at once. A walk-in wants several demand drafts. A logistics partnership wants a current account. And a young engineer says she already has a 'CKYC number'.
(on video from the digital onboarding hub, Kochi) Kavya Reddy here. The CKYC one is easy if we use the registry properly. Don't make her bring a pile of photocopies.
The partnership worries me more. One partner signs everything, but the deed mentions a 'silent partner' in Dubai.
Then we need to know who really owns and controls that firm before we open anything. The PML Rules give us the thresholds.
And the walk-in with the drafts? He keeps asking what the limit is before we need his ID.
Asking about limits is a small red flag on its own. Let's go through the gate rules one by one.

cards.title: What customer due diligence means in India

scenes.heading: Identify and verify
scenes.narration: CDD means identifying the customer and verifying that identity from reliable, independent sources, such as an officially valid document, Aadhaar-based e-KYC or records from the Central KYC Records Registry.

scenes.heading: Purpose and nature
scenes.narration: The bank also gathers the purpose and intended nature of the relationship, so it knows what normal activity should look like later.

scenes.heading: Business, ownership, control
scenes.narration: For businesses, staff take reasonable steps to understand what the customer does and who owns and controls it.

scenes.heading: The real owner
scenes.narration: Staff decide whether the customer acts for a beneficial owner, then identify that natural person and take all reasonable steps to verify who they are.

scenes.heading: One customer, one ID
scenes.narration: CDD applies at the level of the Unique Customer Identification Code. An existing KYC-compliant customer opening another product does not need fresh identification.

cards.title: The onboarding path at Kaveri Meridian
cards.caption: Based on Chapters III, V and VI and paragraph 65 of the RBI KYC Directions 2025.

items.label: Acceptance check
items.detail: No anonymous, fictitious or benami names; screen against the sanctions lists.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Collect the OVD, e-KYC data or KYC Identifier, plus PAN or Form 60.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Check documents with issuing authorities, such as PAN and GST verification facilities.

items.label: Beneficial owner
items.detail: For non-individuals, identify the natural persons who own or control.

items.label: Risk category
items.detail: Assign low, medium or high risk and record the reasons internally.

items.label: Registry
items.detail: Upload KYC records to CKYCR within 10 days and share the KYC Identifier.

cards.question: A walk-in customer with no account wants to buy demand drafts totalling ₹55,000 in one visit. Does the bank need to identify him?
options: Yes: walk-in transactions of ₹50,000 or more, single or connected, need customer identification
No: walk-in customers only need identification above ₹10 lakh
No: demand drafts are bank instruments, so no CDD applies
Only if he pays in cash rather than by cheque
cards.explanation: Paragraph 21 requires identification for walk-in transactions of ₹50,000 or more, whether one transaction or several that appear connected. Separately, drafts of ₹50,000 and above must be paid for by debit to an account or by cheque, not cash.

cards.title: Who is the beneficial owner?
cards.caption: Thresholds from the definition of beneficial owner in the KYC Directions, which follows Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules. Entities listed in India (and their subsidiaries) need not have shareholders identified.

items.label: Company
items.left: Natural person with more than 10% of shares, capital or profits
items.right: Or anyone controlling, e.g. right to appoint most directors

items.label: Partnership firm
items.left: More than 10% of capital or profits
items.right: Or anyone controlling management or policy decisions

items.label: Association or body of individuals
items.left: More than 15% of property, capital or profits
items.right: If no one qualifies: the senior managing official

items.label: Trust
items.left: Author, trustee and beneficiaries with 10% or more interest
items.right: Plus anyone with ultimate effective control

cards.title: CDD now, or not needed?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each request triggers customer identification at that moment.

items.text: A walk-in asks to send ₹8,000 abroad to a relative
A walk-in pays ₹48,000 today and ₹48,000 tomorrow for the same purpose, saying he wants to 'stay under the limit'
An existing KYC-compliant customer opens a fixed deposit
The bank doubts whether a customer's earlier ID data was genuine
A KYC-compliant customer transfers her account to the bank's Nagpur branch
A new company account is opened for a logistics firm
A non-customer pays ₹75,000 of credit card dues at the counter
A KYC-compliant customer adds a debit card to her existing account

cards.title: Documents the bank may accept
cards.body:
**Officially valid documents (OVDs)** are: passport, driving licence, proof of possession of Aadhaar number, Voter ID card, NREGA job card signed by a State Government officer, and the National Population Register letter with name and address.

**When the address is out of date**, some documents count as OVDs for proof of address only, e.g. a utility bill not older than two months, a property or municipal tax receipt, a pension payment order, or an employer's accommodation allotment letter. The customer must then give an OVD with the current address **within three months**.

**Also remember:**
- PAN (or Form 60) is obtained and verified with the issuing authority.
- Aadhaar numbers must be redacted where the Directions say so.
- Banks must not ask for **introductions** when opening accounts.
- A rejection must reflect real thought, and the officer records the reasons. The policy must not shut out the financially or socially disadvantaged, including persons with disabilities.

lines.text: The engineer gave her KYC Identifier, but our new teller still asked for her passport, a utility bill and two photos.
That's exactly what the Directions try to stop. We retrieve her records online with the identifier and only ask for more if something has changed or the record is incomplete.
RBI fined a large private bank in 2026 for not having a system to use the KYC Identifier when opening accounts. This is not a small thing.
Fine. Now the partnership. The local partner refuses to name the silent partner in Dubai.

cards.title: The silent partner
cards.situation: Coastline Logistics, a partnership, wants a current account. The deed shows a Pune partner with 55% and 'a partner resident abroad' with 45%, name withheld. The Pune partner says the Dubai partner 'values privacy' and offers a large fixed deposit if the bank skips this.

choices.text: Explain that the bank must identify and verify every natural person with more than 10% of capital or profits; without it the account cannot be opened, and consider an STR if suspicion arises.
choices.outcome: Correct. The 45% partner is a beneficial owner. If CDD cannot be applied because the customer will not cooperate, the bank must not open the account and should consider an STR.

choices.text: Open the account now and collect the Dubai partner's details at the next periodic updation.
choices.outcome: CDD must be completed before the relationship starts. Deferring beneficial owner identification breaks the Customer Acceptance Policy.

choices.text: Accept a declaration from the Pune partner that the Dubai partner is not a PEP or sanctioned.
choices.outcome: A self-declaration about an unnamed person is not identification or verification. The bank still does not know who the beneficial owner is.

choices.text: Refuse the account politely and close the file without further thought.
choices.outcome: Refusing is right, but the bank should also record the reasons and consider whether the refusal and the incentive offered warrant an STR.

cards.title: Third-party reliance: the conditions
cards.prompt: Match each condition for relying on CDD done by a third party.

pairs.right: The bank obtains the CDD records immediately from the third party or from CKYCR
The bank is satisfied the third party will provide identification copies without delay
The third party is regulated and supervised and has CDD and record-keeping measures
The third party is not based in a country assessed as high-risk
The bank keeps ultimate responsibility for CDD and any enhanced measures

cards.back: Never. No account may be opened in an anonymous, fictitious or benami name.

cards.front: Customer will not cooperate with CDD?
cards.back: Do not open the account, and consider filing an STR.
Apply CDD to every joint account holder.

cards.front: Extra information beyond the KYC policy?
cards.back: Only with the customer's explicit consent.
The policy must spell out when a customer may act on behalf of another person or entity.
The bank needs a system to check that the customer does not match anyone on the lists in Chapter IX.

cards.question: A partnership's deed shows four partners with 30%, 30%, 32% and 8% of profits, and no other control rights. Who are the beneficial owners under the PML Rules test?
options: The three partners with 30%, 30% and 32%
Only the partner with 32%
All four partners
Only the managing partner who signs cheques
cards.explanation: For a partnership, a natural person with more than 10% of capital or profits, or who controls through other means, is a beneficial owner. The 8% partner does not cross the threshold unless he has control rights.

cards.title: Real case: RBI penalises Yes Bank over the KYC Identifier (2026)
cards.body:
By an order dated **27 April 2026**, RBI imposed a monetary penalty of **₹31.80 lakh** on Yes Bank Limited for not complying with certain provisions of its KYC directions.

The statutory inspection looked at the bank's position as on 31 March 2025. After a show-cause notice and a personal hearing, RBI found one charge sustained: the bank had **not put in place a system to use the KYC Identifier** assigned by the Central KYC Records Registry when establishing account-based relationships.

The penalty was imposed under section 47A(1)(c) read with section 46(4)(i) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. As in all such releases, RBI said it was not ruling on the validity of any customer transaction.

**Lesson:** CKYCR is not optional plumbing. Retrieving records with the identifier is a regulatory duty and a better customer experience.

cards.title: Real case: RBI penalises Central Bank of India (2026)
cards.body:
By an order dated **23 March 2026**, RBI imposed a penalty of **₹63.60 lakh** on Central Bank of India for non-compliance with its directions on KYC and on Basic Savings Bank Deposit Accounts.

The sustained charges were that the bank:
- **failed to upload the KYC records of certain customers onto CKYCR within the prescribed timeline**; and
- opened additional BSBD accounts for customers who already held one.

**What the timeline is:** under Rule 9(1A) of the PML Rules, as restated in paragraph 65 of the KYC Directions, the bank must capture and upload a customer's KYC records to CKYCR **within 10 days** of starting the account-based relationship. Updated information obtained later must reach CKYCR within seven days, or any period the Government notifies.

**Lesson:** back-office uploads are part of KYC. A missed batch upload can lead to a penalty just as a missed document does.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: No anonymous, fictitious or benami accounts; no account where CDD cannot be applied, and consider an STR when a customer will not cooperate.
Identify walk-in customers for transactions of ₹50,000 or more (single or connected), for any international money transfer, and whenever structuring is suspected.
Beneficial owner thresholds: more than 10% for companies and partnerships, more than 15% for associations, 10% or more for trust beneficiaries, plus anyone with control.
Use the KYC Identifier to retrieve CKYCR records and upload new KYC records within 10 days of opening the relationship.
Relying on a third party never moves responsibility: the bank keeps ultimate responsibility for CDD.

cards.prompt: Recall the last account you opened or reviewed. Could you name every beneficial owner and show how you verified them? What would you do differently after this stage?

quiz.question: Under the KYC Directions, what is the threshold for identifying a walk-in customer (no account) for an ordinary transaction?
options: More than ₹10 lakh in cash in a single transaction
₹2 lakh or more, counting only single transactions
₹50,000 or more, whether one transaction or several that appear connected
Any amount above ₹25,000 paid in cash
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 21 sets ₹50,000 or more, single or connected, for walk-in customers. ₹10 lakh is the cash transaction reporting threshold in the PML Rules, which is a different duty.

quiz.question: A walk-in customer who has no account asks the bank to remit ₹6,000 to a cousin in Singapore. What does the bank need to do?
options: Nothing, because the amount is below ₹50,000
Identify the customer, because any international money transfer for a non-account holder needs identification
Only record the cousin's name and bank details
Identify the customer only if he pays in cash
quiz.explanation: Identification is required for any international money transfer operation for a person who is not an account holder, regardless of amount.

quiz.question: A company customer's shareholding shows: holding company A with 60% (owned 100% by Mr Rao), and five individuals with 8% each. Who is the beneficial owner?
options: Mr Rao, who controls more than 10% through holding company A
Holding company A, as the largest shareholder
All five individuals, as together they hold 40%
Nobody, because no individual holds shares directly
quiz.explanation: Beneficial owners are natural persons who hold more than 10% acting alone or together, or through other legal persons. Mr Rao controls 60% through A. Each individual holds 8% and, absent a control arrangement, is below the threshold.

quiz.question: A customer will not provide documents needed for CDD and becomes evasive when asked about the source of an initial deposit. What does the Customer Acceptance Policy require?
options: Open the account with a low balance limit until documents arrive
Do not open the account, and consider filing an STR
Open the account if a senior manager approves an exception
Refer the customer to another bank and take no further action
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 17 says the bank must not open an account where it cannot apply CDD because of non-cooperation or unreliable information, and should consider an STR.

quiz.question: Within what time must the bank upload a new customer's KYC records to the Central KYC Records Registry?
options: Within 30 days of the start of the relationship
Within 15 days of the end of the month
At the first periodic updation of KYC
Within 10 days of the start of the account-based relationship
quiz.explanation: Rule 9(1A) of the PML Rules, restated in paragraph 65, requires upload within 10 days of commencing the account-based relationship. RBI penalised Central Bank of India in 2026 for missing this timeline.

quiz.question: A customer gives her KYC Identifier. The records retrieved from CKYCR are complete and current. What should the branch do?
options: Ask for fresh OVD copies anyway, to keep a branch file
Ask her to visit the branch with two introducers
Rely on the CKYCR records and not ask her to resubmit the same documents
Restart CDD because CKYCR data cannot be relied on
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 65 says the bank should use the KYC Identifier to obtain records and not require the customer to submit them again unless information has changed, the record is incomplete or not current, or similar exceptions apply.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an officially valid document (OVD) under the KYC Directions?
options: A PAN card
A bank passbook from another bank
A college identity card
A job card issued under NREGA and signed by a State Government officer
quiz.explanation: The OVD list is passport, driving licence, proof of possession of Aadhaar number, Voter ID, NREGA job card signed by a State Government officer, and the NPR letter. PAN is collected and verified separately.

quiz.question: A customer's passport shows a Delhi address but she lives in Chennai and provides a two-month-old electricity bill for the Chennai address. What applies?
options: The bill can serve as a deemed OVD for address, and she must give an OVD with the current address within three months
The account cannot be opened until she updates her passport
The bill is enough permanently and no further document is needed
The bank must verify the address only at periodic updation
quiz.explanation: A utility bill not more than two months old is deemed an OVD for proof of address only, and the customer must submit an OVD with the current address within three months.

quiz.question: Kaveri Meridian wants to rely on CDD done by an insurance company that is regulated in India. Which statement is correct?
options: Once it relies on the insurer, responsibility for CDD moves to the insurer
Reliance is allowed only if FIU-IND approves each case
Reliance is never allowed for account-based relationships
The bank may rely on it under conditions, but it keeps ultimate responsibility for CDD
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 22 allows reliance on a regulated third party subject to conditions, including getting the records immediately and the third party not being in a high-risk country. The bank remains ultimately responsible.

quiz.question: For a trust, which persons must the bank identify as beneficial owners?
options: Only the trustees who sign the account opening form
The author, the trustee, beneficiaries with 10% or more interest and anyone with ultimate effective control
Only beneficiaries with more than 25% interest
Only the author of the trust and the managing trustee
quiz.explanation: For trusts the definition covers the author, the trustee, beneficiaries with 10% or more interest and any natural person exercising ultimate effective control.

sessions.title: Risk categorisation, V-CIP, enhanced due diligence and periodic updation
sessions.summary: Categorise customers by risk and review them every six months, run video-based customer identification (V-CIP) to RBI's standards, apply enhanced due diligence to non-face-to-face customers and PEPs, monitor accounts and keep KYC up to date on the 2-8-10 year cycle.
objectives: Categorise customers as low, medium or high risk and keep the category confidential
Explain the V-CIP standards, including why only specially trained officials may run it
Apply enhanced due diligence to non-face-to-face onboarding and to politically exposed persons
Carry out ongoing due diligence and periodic updation of KYC within RBI's minimum periods

cards.title: Stage three: the risk ledger
cards.setting: Digital onboarding hub, Kaveri Meridian Bank, Kakkanad, Kochi. 3:40 pm.

lines.text: Come and watch this V-CIP call. The customer keeps glancing to the left before every answer.
On screen, a man answers questions about his occupation. A faint second voice can be heard just before he speaks.
I changed the order of my questions twice. Each time he pauses and someone off-camera whispers.
That is prompting. The Directions are clear: if the official sees prompting at the customer's end, the account opening is rejected.
This is why RBI says only specially trained officials may run V-CIP. A script cannot spot this. People can.
And when you're done, I have 2,300 accounts due for their six-monthly risk review. Anyone want to help?

scenes.heading: What V-CIP is
scenes.narration: Video-based Customer Identification is a live, consent-based audio-visual interaction in which an authorised bank official identifies the customer. Done to RBI's standards, it counts the same as face-to-face identification.

scenes.heading: Trained officials only
scenes.narration: Only officials specially trained for V-CIP may run it. They must be able to check liveness and detect manipulation or suspicious behaviour, and act on what they see.

scenes.heading: Real time, not recorded
scenes.narration: The official varies the order and type of questions to show the call is live. If someone is prompting the customer, the account opening is rejected.

scenes.heading: Secure by design
scenes.narration: Calls start from the bank's own secured network, block IP addresses outside India or spoofed ones, and carry GPS co-ordinates with a date and time stamp.

scenes.heading: Audit before use
scenes.narration: The official captures a photo, matches it with the Aadhaar or OVD and PAN, and the account becomes operational only after concurrent audit. Recordings are stored in India.

cards.question: During a V-CIP call, the official hears someone off-camera telling the customer how to answer. What should happen?
options: The bank rejects the account opening process
The official notes it and completes the account opening
The call continues after the other person leaves the room
The customer is asked to come to a branch within three days to finish
cards.explanation: Paragraph 27 says the bank shall reject the account opening process if it observes any prompting at the customer's end.

cards.title: The clocks in RBI's KYC Directions
cards.caption: Minimum frequencies counted from account opening or the last KYC updation (paragraphs 41 and 42). A bank's Board-approved policy can set shorter periods.

items.label: Risk category review
items.detail: Banks review the risk categorisation of accounts at least once every six months.

items.label: High-risk customers
items.detail: Periodic updation of KYC at least once every two years.

items.label: Medium-risk customers
items.detail: Periodic updation at least once every eight years.

items.label: Low-risk customers
items.detail: Periodic updation at least once every ten years.

cards.title: Enhanced measures or standard?
cards.prompt: Decide whether each customer needs enhanced due diligence or monitoring under the KYC Directions.

items.text: A customer onboarded remotely through DigiLocker documents, not yet verified face to face or by V-CIP
The brother of a serving foreign head of government opens an account
A multi-level marketing firm receives many small cash deposits across the country
A salaried teacher whose account was opened through a fully compliant V-CIP
An existing customer becomes a senior executive of a foreign state-owned corporation
A pensioner whose account receives only monthly pension credits
An NRI onboarded with an OVD copy certified by a notary abroad

cards.title: PEPs under RBI's Directions
The six-month backlog
cards.setting: Transaction monitoring room, BKC, Mumbai. 6:15 pm.

lines.text: Some of these accounts haven't had their risk category reviewed for over a year. The system was switched off during a migration.
Then we have a regulatory breach to fix, not just a backlog. RBI has penalised banks in 2026 for not having a system of periodic risk review at all.
And one of the accounts belongs to Mr Anand Pillai. Long-time NRI customer in Port Louis. He was just appointed a minister in Mauritius.
Then he is now a PEP for us. Before we decide anything, think about what the Directions require.

cards.title: A customer becomes a PEP
cards.situation: Mr Pillai has banked with Kaveri Meridian for 12 years: an NRE account, two fixed deposits and a home loan in Kochi. News reports confirm his appointment as a minister in Mauritius. His relationship manager says: 'He is a good customer; nothing has changed.'

choices.text: Flag him as a PEP, seek senior management approval to continue, establish source of funds and wealth, and put the accounts under enhanced monitoring.
choices.outcome: Correct. When an existing customer becomes a PEP, the bank needs senior management approval to continue, reasonable measures on source of funds and wealth, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.

choices.text: Close all his accounts immediately because PEPs are too risky.
choices.outcome: The Directions let banks serve PEPs with the right controls. Closing a long-standing relationship without assessment is not what the rules require.

choices.text: Keep the relationship as it is and review it at his next periodic updation.
choices.outcome: A change to PEP status needs action now: senior management approval and enhanced monitoring cannot wait for the next updation cycle.

choices.text: Raise the risk category to high, but leave approval to the relationship manager.
choices.outcome: Raising the risk category is right, but approval to continue must come from senior management, not the relationship manager.

cards.title: Remote onboarding: two routes
cards.caption: Paragraphs 27 and 44 of the KYC Directions. Aadhaar OTP-based e-KYC accounts follow their own conditions in paragraph 25.

items.label: Status
items.left: On par with face-to-face if all V-CIP standards are met
items.right: Enhanced due diligence applies

items.label: Offer first?
items.left: Must be offered first for remote onboarding where the bank has V-CIP
items.right: Used where V-CIP is not chosen

items.label: Risk category
items.left: Set by the normal risk assessment
items.right: High risk until verified face to face or by V-CIP

items.label: First transaction
items.left: No special rule
items.right: Must be a credit from the customer's existing KYC-compliant bank account

items.label: Address and mobile
items.left: Captured during the call
items.right: Positive address confirmation before operations; transactions only from the mobile number used at opening

cards.title: V-CIP: what the official must know

cards.back: Only bank officials specially trained for it, able to check liveness and detect fraudulent manipulation or suspicious conduct.

cards.front: Can liveness checks exclude a customer with special needs?
cards.back: No. The bank must take account of special needs, and the liveness check must not exclude persons with special needs.
No. After a call drop or disconnection, a fresh session must be started.

cards.front: Customer shows a printed copy of his e-PAN.
cards.back: Not valid. Printed copies of equivalent e-documents, including e-PAN, cannot be used for V-CIP.

cards.front: Aadhaar XML file downloaded four working days ago?
cards.back: Too old. The XML file or Secure QR code must not be older than three working days on the day of V-CIP.
Report it as a cyber event under the regulatory guidelines and use the lessons to update the technology and workflows.

cards.title: Periodic updation for a change of address
cards.prompt: Put the steps for an individual customer who has only changed address in the right order.
steps: Send at least three advance intimations before the due date, at least one by letter
Receive the customer's self-declaration of the new address through a registered channel
Give the customer an acknowledgement showing the date of receipt
Verify the declared address by positive confirmation within two months
Update the records promptly and send the updated KYC to CKYCR
Inform the customer of the date on which the KYC details were updated

cards.question: Kaveri Meridian classifies a trading company as high risk. What is the latest point by which its KYC must next be updated under the Directions?
options: Two years from account opening or the last KYC updation
Six months from account opening or the last updation
Eight years from account opening or the last updation
Only when the company reports a change in its documents
cards.explanation: Periodic updation is at least every two years for high-risk, eight for medium-risk and ten for low-risk customers. Six months is the minimum frequency for reviewing risk categorisation, which is a different duty.

cards.title: Real case: RBI penalises a central co-operative bank (2026)
cards.body:
By an order dated **3 June 2026**, RBI imposed a penalty of **₹3 lakh** on The Karnal Central Cooperative Bank Limited, Haryana, for not complying with its KYC directions.

NABARD's statutory inspection looked at the bank's position as on 31 March 2025. After a show-cause notice and hearing, RBI found that the bank had failed to:
- put in place a **system of periodic review of risk categorisation** of accounts; and
- put in place **robust software** to identify and report suspicious transactions.

In 2026 RBI also penalised several NBFCs on the same point, e.g. Fusion Finance Limited (₹2.70 lakh, order dated 14 August 2026), for having no system to review risk categorisation at least every six months.

**Lesson:** risk categories are not set once at onboarding. Without a working six-monthly review, risk-based monitoring and periodic updation both fail.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Customers are categorised low, medium or high risk; the category and the reasons stay confidential to avoid tipping off.
Risk categorisation is reviewed at least every six months; KYC is updated at least every 2, 8 and 10 years for high, medium and low risk.
V-CIP is run only by specially trained officials; prompting means rejection, and accounts become operational only after concurrent audit.
Non-face-to-face customers not onboarded by V-CIP are high risk until verified, and their first transaction must come from their own KYC-compliant account.
Foreign PEPs, their families and close associates need senior management approval, source of funds and wealth checks and enhanced monitoring.

cards.prompt: If you were asked to run or supervise a V-CIP call tomorrow, what three warning signs would you watch for, and what would you do the moment you saw one?

quiz.question: How often, at a minimum, must a bank review the risk categorisation of its customers' accounts?
options: At least once a year
At least once every six months
At least once every two years
Only at periodic updation of KYC
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 41 requires a system of periodic review of risk categorisation at least once every six months. RBI has penalised banks and NBFCs in 2026 for lacking such a system.

quiz.question: A customer asks why the bank has placed him in the 'high risk' category. What should the staff member do?
options: Explain that the bank cannot share risk categorisation details, without revealing the category or reasons
Tell him the category and the reasons, as he is entitled to know
Lower the category if he provides a written explanation
Show him the internal risk scoring sheet on request
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 20 requires the bank to keep the risk category and the reasons confidential and not reveal them to the customer, to avoid tipping off.

quiz.question: Which statement about V-CIP is correct under the KYC Directions?
options: Only bank officials specially trained for V-CIP may conduct it
Any customer service agent may run it if the call is recorded
The customer must blink and smile for the liveness check to pass
It may be run from a vendor's premises outside the bank's network
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 27 limits V-CIP to specially trained officials. Specific gestures are not mandatory for liveness, and calls must originate from the bank's own secured network.

quiz.question: Ms Fernandes opened her account remotely using DigiLocker documents, not by V-CIP. A week later she asks to link her husband's mobile number for transaction OTPs. What should the bank do?
options: Link it, as spouses may share OTP numbers
Link it after a one-time OTP to the original number
Decline: transactions are permitted only from the mobile number used for account opening
Link it once she has made three successful transactions
quiz.explanation: For non-face-to-face onboarding under paragraph 44, alternate mobile numbers must not be linked after CDD for transaction OTPs or updates; transactions are allowed only from the number used at opening.

quiz.question: Under the KYC Directions, which person is a PEP?
options: A municipal ward clerk in Pune
A senior judge in Kenya who opens an account with the bank's Mumbai branch
A retired schoolteacher whose cousin is a local councillor in India
A junior officer in a foreign embassy's visa section
quiz.explanation: The Directions define PEPs as individuals entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country, including senior judicial officers. Junior or local roles do not meet the definition, though a bank's own policy may go further.

quiz.question: An existing customer becomes a PEP. What must the bank obtain to continue the relationship?
options: Senior management approval
FIU-IND's written consent
A fresh introduction from another customer
Approval from the branch manager only
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 45 requires senior management approval to continue the relationship when an existing customer or beneficial owner becomes a PEP.

quiz.question: A low-risk individual's periodic KYC updation is due but he has not yet responded. What do the Directions say about his account?
options: The bank allows all transactions while it completes updation within the permitted time, with regular monitoring
The bank freezes the account until he updates his KYC
The bank closes the account after the first reminder
The bank allows only credits until he updates his KYC
quiz.explanation: For low-risk individuals, paragraph 42 lets all transactions continue while updation is completed within one year of falling due (or by 30 June 2026 if later), with regular monitoring.

quiz.question: Before the due date of periodic updation, what notice must the bank give the customer?
options: One email at least 30 days before the due date
A single letter sent by registered post
No notice: the customer must track the due date
At least three advance intimations, at least one of them by letter
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 42(7) requires at least three advance intimations, including at least one by letter, and at least three reminders after the due date, including one by letter.

quiz.question: An individual tells the bank through his registered email that only his address has changed. What must the bank do with the new address?
options: Verify it through positive confirmation within two months
Accept it without verification, as the email is registered
Ask him to open a new account at the new address
Verify it at the next periodic updation
quiz.explanation: For a change in address only, the bank takes a self-declaration through a registered channel and verifies the address by positive confirmation within two months.

quiz.question: Which type of transaction does paragraph 40 of the KYC Directions specifically require banks to monitor?
options: Salary credits from a listed employer
Standing instructions for utility bills
Deposits of third-party cheques followed by large cash withdrawals
Interest credits on fixed deposits
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 40 lists large and complex transactions (including RTGS) with unusual patterns, threshold breaches, high turnover inconsistent with balances, and third-party cheque deposits followed by large cash withdrawals.

sessions.title: Reporting to FIU-IND, tipping off, monitoring and records
sessions.summary: Know every report a bank sends to FIU-IND (CTR, CBWTR, NTR, counterfeit currency and STR), the deadlines in Rule 8, filing through FINnet 2.0, the confidentiality and tipping-off rules, money mule accounts, alert software and the PMLA record-keeping periods.
objectives: Identify which transactions must be reported to FIU-IND and by when under Rules 3 and 8 of the PML Rules
Recognise a suspicious transaction under the Indian definition, including attempted transactions
Avoid tipping off and keep the fact of reporting confidential, without restricting accounts merely because an STR was filed
Apply the five-year record-keeping rules and RBI's expectations on money mules and alert software

cards.title: Stage four: the signal room
cards.setting: Transaction monitoring room, BKC, Mumbai. 10:05 am.

lines.text: Look at this cluster. Fourteen new savings accounts, mostly students, opened in the last two months. Each gets dozens of small UPI credits, then cash goes out at ATMs within hours.
Classic money mule pattern. Someone is renting these accounts to move fraud proceeds.
The alert system flagged them three weeks ago. The first reviewer closed the alerts as 'student activity'.
That is exactly what FIU-IND criticised at a public sector bank in 2024: alerts closed with minimal justification and almost no STRs filed.
And the Directions are blunt: if an account turns out to be a mule and we never filed an STR, RBI deems us non-compliant.
So we reopen, investigate and get this to you for a decision today.

scenes.heading: Alerts
scenes.narration: The bank must run robust software that raises alerts when transactions do not fit the customer's risk category and updated profile. RBI encourages banks to consider AI and machine learning tools to support monitoring.

scenes.heading: Investigation
scenes.narration: Analysts review the alert against what the bank knows: the customer's business, risk profile and source of funds. Closing an alert needs a real reason on file.

scenes.heading: Principal Officer's decision
scenes.narration: When the Principal Officer is satisfied a transaction is suspicious, the PML Rules require the information to be furnished promptly to the Director, FIU-IND.

scenes.heading: Filing
scenes.narration: Reports are filed in FIU-IND's prescribed formats through its FINnet 2.0 system, using the FINGate 2.0 portal on which reporting entities are registered.

scenes.heading: Silence
scenes.narration: Everyone in the bank keeps the fact of reporting confidential. The customer is never told, and the account is not restricted merely because an STR was filed.

cards.title: The reports a bank sends to FIU-IND
cards.caption: Rules 3 and 8 of the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005. Each day of delay in reporting or in correcting a misreported transaction is a separate violation.

items.label: Cash Transaction Report (CTR)
items.left: Cash over ₹10 lakh, or connected cash transactions in a month that together exceed ₹10 lakh
items.right: Monthly, by the 15th of the next month

items.label: Cross-Border Wire Transfer Report
items.left: Cross-border wire transfers over ₹5 lakh where the origin or destination is in India
items.right: Monthly, by the 15th of the next month

items.label: NPO Transaction Report
items.left: Receipts by non-profit organisations of more than ₹10 lakh
items.right: Monthly, by the 15th of the next month

items.label: Counterfeit Currency Report
items.left: Cash transactions using forged or counterfeit notes, or forged securities or documents
items.right: Monthly, by the 15th of the next month

items.label: Suspicious Transaction Report (STR)
items.left: Any suspicious transaction, attempted or executed, cash or not, of any value
items.right: Promptly, once the Principal Officer is satisfied it is suspicious

cards.question: A customer deposits ₹4 lakh in cash on the 3rd, ₹3.5 lakh on the 12th and ₹3 lakh on the 25th of the same month, all for his trading business. What does Rule 3 require?
options: Report the series in the monthly CTR, because connected cash transactions in the month exceed ₹10 lakh
Nothing, because no single deposit exceeds ₹10 lakh
File an STR immediately, because splitting cash is always suspicious
Report only the largest deposit in the next CTR
cards.explanation: Rule 3 covers a series of integrally connected cash transactions individually below ₹10 lakh within a month whose total exceeds ₹10 lakh. Splitting can be a red flag, but a CTR duty arises regardless; an STR depends on the facts.

cards.title: CTR, STR or neither?
cards.prompt: Choose the right reporting route for each situation at Kaveri Meridian.

items.text: A jeweller deposits ₹12 lakh in cash in one go, consistent with his known business
A customer abandons a ₹3 lakh transfer when asked for the source of funds and leaves
A new student account receives 40 small UPI credits a day, withdrawn in cash within hours
An exporter receives an ₹8 lakh wire from a foreign buyer, matching its invoices
A salaried customer pays her ₹18,000 credit card bill from her salary account
A shell-like firm with ₹1 lakh capital shows crores of RTGS turnover passing on the same day
A pensioner withdraws ₹20,000 in cash for household expenses

cards.title: Tipping off and protection for reporters
cards.body:
**Confidentiality.** Under PMLA section 12 and Rule 8, the bank, its directors, officers and all employees must keep confidential the fact that records are maintained and information is furnished to FIU-IND. Group-wide information sharing must include safeguards against tipping off.

**Do not alert the customer.** If staff suspect money laundering or terrorist financing and reasonably believe that carrying on with CDD would tip off the customer, the Directions say **stop the CDD and file an STR** instead. The customer's risk category and the reasons for it are also kept confidential.

**Do not punish on the STR alone.** The bank must not restrict operations in an account merely because an STR has been filed. Any restriction needs its own legal basis, such as a freezing order.

**Protection.** Section 14 of the PMLA says the bank, its directors and employees are not liable to civil or criminal proceedings for furnishing information to FIU-IND under section 12, except as section 13 provides.

lines.text: One of the mule accounts belongs to a student who walked in today to withdraw cash. My teller wants to ask her outright: 'Are you renting out your account?'
Careful. An STR is being prepared on that account. Questions that hint at a report could tip her off.
Then should we just block the account until FIU-IND replies?
Not merely because of the STR. If there are fraud complaints or a legal order, those are separate grounds. Let's think it through.

cards.title: Handling the customer under an STR
cards.situation: The student asks to withdraw ₹45,000 in cash. The STR on her account will be filed today. There is no freezing order, no fraud complaint naming her account, and her KYC is complete.

choices.text: Process the request normally, record any unusual behaviour for the Principal Officer, and say nothing about monitoring or reports.
choices.outcome: Correct. The fact of reporting stays confidential, and the bank must not restrict the account merely because an STR is filed. New observations go to the Principal Officer to update the case.

choices.text: Refuse the withdrawal and tell her the account is under review by FIU-IND.
choices.outcome: This tips her off and restricts the account solely because of the STR, both of which the rules prohibit.

choices.text: Ask her detailed questions about who controls the account before paying.
choices.outcome: Normal questions are fine, but probing that signals suspicion can tip her off. Her KYC is complete, so heavy questioning now adds risk without legal need.

choices.text: Delay the payment until the STR is filed, then pay without explanation.
choices.outcome: An unexplained delay tied to the STR is still a restriction based on the report, and it may alert the customer.

cards.title: The STR path at Kaveri Meridian
cards.prompt: Put the steps in the order they should happen.
steps: Alert software flags transactions that do not match the customer's risk profile
An analyst investigates and records reasons, escalating if suspicion remains
The case goes to the Principal Officer with the evidence gathered
The Principal Officer decides the transaction is suspicious
The STR is filed promptly with FIU-IND through its reporting portal
The case file is kept confidential and retained under the PMLA record rules

cards.back: No. Proceeds of a scheduled offence can be suspicious regardless of the value involved.

cards.front: Does the transaction need to complete?
cards.back: No. Attempted transactions are included, so a customer who walks away can still be reported.
No. Suspicious transactions can be in cash or by any other means, including electronic transfers.
A transaction made in circumstances of unusual or unjustified complexity can be suspicious.

cards.question: The Principal Officer is satisfied on 9 June that a transaction is suspicious. When must the STR be furnished to FIU-IND?
options: By 15 July, with the monthly reports
Promptly, once she is satisfied that it is suspicious
Within 30 days of the transaction date
At the end of the quarter, with other STRs
cards.explanation: Rule 8(2) requires the Principal Officer to furnish suspicious transaction information promptly once satisfied it is suspicious. The 15th-of-the-month deadline applies to CTRs and other threshold reports.

cards.title: Real case: FIU-IND fines Union Bank of India ₹54 lakh (2024)
cards.body:
After an observation by FIU-IND, a review of **Union Bank of India** found current accounts at a Mumbai branch used by an NBFC and associated entities for heavy **circular fund transfers**. The entities shared a registered address and beneficial owners, had authorised capital of only ₹1 lakh each, yet showed turnover far beyond their declared business, mainly RTGS inflows passed quickly to group entities.

Only **one STR** had been filed despite the volumes, and many **alerts were closed with minimal justification**.

By Order-in-Original No. 13/DIR/FIU-IND/2024 (October 2024), the Director imposed **₹54 lakh** for failing to report STRs, to carry out ongoing due diligence, to review CDD and to run an internal mechanism to detect and report suspicious transactions. FIU-IND also directed a review of due diligence and of how alerts are closed.

**Lesson:** a closed alert without reasons is a reporting failure waiting to be found.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: CTR, cross-border wire transfer, NPO and counterfeit currency reports are monthly, due by the 15th of the next month; STRs go promptly once the Principal Officer is satisfied.
Thresholds: cash over ₹10 lakh (single or connected within a month), cross-border wires over ₹5 lakh, NPO receipts over ₹10 lakh. STRs have no threshold.
Each day of delay in reporting or correcting a report is a separate violation.
Never tip off: keep reporting confidential, stop CDD and file an STR if CDD would alert the customer, and do not restrict an account merely because of an STR.
Keep transaction records five years from the transaction and identity records five years after the relationship ends; a mule account with no STR means the bank is deemed non-compliant.

options: By the 15th day of the following month
By the 7th working day of the following month
By the last day of the following month
Within 30 days of each cash transaction
quiz.explanation: Rule 8(1) requires the Principal Officer to furnish CTR and other monthly threshold information by the 15th of the succeeding month.

quiz.question: A customer starts a ₹2 lakh cash deposit, but cancels it when the cashier asks for his PAN, saying he will 'come back with a smaller amount'. What should the bank consider?
options: Nothing, because the transaction was never completed
An STR, because attempted transactions are covered and the behaviour suggests avoidance
A CTR, because the cash was presented at the counter
Closing his account immediately without any report
quiz.explanation: The definition of suspicious transaction includes attempted transactions of any value. A CTR applies only to cash over ₹10 lakh, and closing the account is not the required response.

quiz.question: An STR has been filed on a customer. She then asks to transfer funds to her own account at another bank. There is no freezing order. What is correct?
options: The bank must block all debits until FIU-IND responds
The bank must tell her that a report was filed before acting
The bank must not restrict the account merely because an STR was filed
The bank must close the account within seven days
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 54 says the bank shall not restrict operations merely on the basis of an STR, and the fact of reporting must stay confidential.

quiz.question: During onboarding, a teller grows suspicious that the applicant is a front for someone else and believes further CDD questions would alert him. What do the Directions require?
options: Complete CDD fully and then decide whether to report
Stop the CDD process and file an STR
Ask the applicant directly whether he is acting for someone else
Open the account and monitor it closely for six months
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 19 says that where the bank suspects ML or TF and reasonably believes CDD would tip off the customer, it should not pursue CDD and should file an STR instead.

quiz.question: Which cross-border wire transfers must be reported to FIU-IND in the monthly report under Rule 3?
options: All cross-border wire transfers of any value
Those of more than ₹5 lakh where the origin or destination of funds is in India
Only outward transfers above ₹10 lakh
Only transfers involving high-risk countries
quiz.explanation: Rule 3(1)(E) covers cross-border wire transfers of more than ₹5 lakh, or the foreign currency equivalent, where either the origin or the destination is in India.

quiz.question: Kaveri Meridian closes a customer's account in March 2026. Until when, at least, must it keep the customer's identification records?
options: Until at least March 2029
Until at least the end of 2026
Until at least March 2036
Until at least March 2031
quiz.explanation: Identification records must be kept for at least five years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later.

quiz.question: An investigation proves that an account opened at Kaveri Meridian was operated as a money mule, but no STR was ever filed. What is the consequence under the KYC Directions?
options: No consequence if the bank closes the account promptly
Only the account-opening officer is held responsible
The bank is deemed not to have complied with the Directions
The bank must refund the defrauded victims in full
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 68 says that if an account is established to be a money mule but the bank did not file an STR, the bank is deemed not to have complied with the Directions.

quiz.question: A CTR for the previous month was filed late by four days. How does Rule 8 treat the delay?
options: The delay is excused if the report was eventually filed
The four days count together as one violation
Each day of delay counts as a separate violation
Delays are treated as violations only for STRs
quiz.explanation: Rule 8(4) and paragraph 54 say each day of delay in reporting, or in correcting a misreported transaction, is a separate violation.

quiz.question: A branch employee files an STR in good faith and the customer threatens to sue her for defamation. What protection does the PMLA give?
options: None; she must rely on the bank's insurance policy
Protection applies only to the Principal Officer, not to other staff
Section 14 protects the bank and its employees from civil or criminal proceedings for furnishing the information
Protection applies only if FIU-IND later confirms the suspicion
quiz.explanation: Section 14 says the reporting entity, its directors and employees are not liable to civil or criminal proceedings for furnishing information under section 12(1)(b), except as section 13 provides.

quiz.question: In its 2024 order against Union Bank of India, which practice did FIU-IND criticise?
options: Filing too many defensive STRs on low-risk customers
Sharing STRs with the customer's auditors
Uploading KYC records to CKYCR late
Closing alerts with minimal justification while filing only one STR
quiz.explanation: FIU-IND's order summary notes that only one STR was filed despite high volumes and that alerts were closed with minimal justification. It imposed ₹54 lakh.

sessions.title: Sanctions, wire transfers, correspondent banking and programme readiness
sessions.summary: Screen against the UNSC and Government of India lists under UAPA section 51A and WMD Act section 12A, carry complete originator and beneficiary data on wire transfers, run correspondent banking due diligence, and bring the bank's whole AML/CFT programme together for audit and the final exam.
objectives: Apply the daily list checks and match procedures under UAPA section 51A, WMD Act section 12A and the UNSCR 1718 Order
State the information that must travel with cross-border and domestic wire transfers, and each bank's role in the chain
Carry out correspondent banking due diligence, including the shell bank prohibition and approvals
Summarise the programme RBI expects: risk assessment, policy, audit, training and regulatory recap

cards.title: Stage five: the final audit
cards.setting: Financial institutions desk, Kaveri Meridian Bank, Connaught Place, New Delhi. 8:45 am.

lines.text: Internal audit starts its AML review on Monday. As Designated Director, I want to walk in knowing every gap.
Three areas worry me: sanctions screening, wire transfer data and a new correspondent request from an offshore bank.
The sanctions team flagged an overnight update to the UN list. Our screening ran at 6 am, so we're covered for today.
And the payments team says some inward SWIFT messages arrive with the originator's address missing. They've been processing them anyway.
Then let's go through each one. By Monday I want answers, not surprises.

scenes.heading: UAPA section 51A
scenes.narration: Banks must not hold accounts for individuals or entities on the UN Security Council's ISIL and Al-Qaida list or the Taliban list, or in the schedules to the 2007 Order that implements Security Council resolutions.

scenes.heading: Every single day
scenes.narration: Banks verify these lists daily and take every addition, deletion or change into account. Accounts resembling listed names are reported to FIU-IND and the Ministry of Home Affairs is advised, following the UAPA Order of 2 February 2021.

scenes.heading: WMD Act section 12A
scenes.narration: Under the Finance Ministry's Order of 1 September 2023, banks must not carry out transactions for persons on the designated list, and must check customers at onboarding and periodically. The Director, FIU-IND is the Central Nodal Officer.

scenes.heading: UNSCR 1718
scenes.narration: Banks also check the UNSCR 1718 list on North Korea every day and comply with the Government's 2017 Order implementing it.

scenes.heading: FATF-listed countries
scenes.narration: For countries the FATF calls out, banks apply effective, proportionate enhanced due diligence, examine the background and purpose of transactions and keep written findings, while legitimate trade can continue.

cards.title: A match under WMD Act section 12A
cards.caption: Paragraph 57 of the KYC Directions, which applies the Order of 1 September 2023. For UAPA matches, follow the 2021 Order reproduced in Annex I of the Directions.

items.label: Screen
items.detail: Check customers at onboarding and periodically against the designated list on FIU-IND's portal.

items.label: Stop
items.detail: Do not carry out any transaction where the particulars match the designated list.

items.detail: Immediately send full particulars of the funds or assets to the Central Nodal Officer (Director, FIU-IND).

items.label: Copy
items.detail: Send a copy to the State Nodal Officer where the account is held and to RBI.

items.label: Freeze
items.detail: On a freezing order from the CNO, act without delay.

items.label: Unfreezing requests
items.detail: Forward any unfreezing application with asset details to the CNO within two working days.

cards.question: How often must a bank verify the UNSC sanctions lists and the lists in the schedules to the 2007 Order under the KYC Directions?
options: Weekly
Monthly, with the CTR
Daily
Only when RBI circulates an update
cards.explanation: Paragraph 56 requires the bank to verify these lists on a daily basis and take additions, deletions and changes into account. Paragraph 58 also requires daily checks of the UNSCR 1718 list.
